content: It is critical to share the genetic sequence data of viruses in publicly accessible databases, such as GISAID or GenBank, when laboratories have the capacity to perform such sequencing. National influenza centers (NICs) may occasionally receive influenza viruses that do not fall into the categories of human seasonal viruses or PIP biological materials, such as viruses derived from animal or environmental specimens. These materials should ideally be handled in facilities separate from those used for investigating human specimens and viruses. NICs are responsible for sharing virus samples with WHO Collaborating Centres (CCs) of the Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System (GISRS) to support risk assessment, adhering to national and international regulations. NICs must ensure that appropriate permits and documentation are in place to facilitate virus sharing. Healthcare facilities must be prepared to manage patients with zoonotic influenza. This includes implementing early infection prevention and control measures to prevent nosocomial transmission, raising awareness among healthcare workers about suspected cases, and establishing screening and triaging systems in hospitals. Standard and droplet precautions, as well as airborne precautions (e.g., N95/FFP2/FFP3 masks), should be implemented during aerosol-generating procedures. Healthcare workers should be monitored for fever and influenza-like illness, provided with personal protective equipment, and trained in its proper use. For clinical management, patients with laboratory-confirmed influenza virus infection who exhibit progressive, complicated, or severe illness—or those at increased risk of severe disease—should be treated with oseltamivir as soon as possible. If laboratory test results are delayed by more than 24 hours, empiric treatment with oseltamivir is recommended and can be adjusted once test results are available. Corticosteroids should not be routinely used but may be considered in cases of septic shock with suspected adrenal insufficiency or co-infection with SARS-CoV-2 in hypoxemic patients. Antibiotic chemoprophylaxis should not be used unless bacterial co-infection, such as bacterial pneumonia or sepsis, is suspected. If empiric antibiotics are initiated, they should be discontinued promptly if microbiological findings are negative. Early recognition and optimized supportive care are essential for treating patients with progressive or severe influenza virus infection. This includes triage, clinical assessments, monitoring oxygen saturation, and providing supplemental oxygen to correct hypoxemia. For patients with acute respiratory distress, advanced non-invasive respiratory support and invasive mechanical ventilation should follow lung-protective strategies. Additional guidance can be found in WHO COVID-19 clinical guidelines and the WHO toolkit for severe acute respiratory infections. All laboratory-confirmed cases of zoonotic influenza must be reported to WHO under the International Health Regulations (IHR, 2005) through the IHR national focal point. WHO updates its recommendations twice a year regarding the need for additional candidate vaccine viruses (CVVs) for pandemic preparedness. Vaccines against zoonotic influenza viruses, such as A(H5N1), have been developed and licensed in several countries but are not widely available. The decision to use these vaccines depends on the risk of infection and national authority decisions. Some countries stockpile these vaccines as part of their pandemic preparedness measures. However, the production of a pandemic influenza vaccine can only begin once the specific pandemic virus strain has been identified. Using current manufacturing technologies, the first doses of a pandemic vaccine would become available 4–6 months after the identification of the pandemic strain. Seasonal influenza vaccination is recommended for healthcare workers in all countries to protect their patients. Vaccination for selected groups at increased risk of exposure to animal influenza viruses may also reduce the probability of human co-infections with both animal and human influenza viruses, thereby decreasing opportunities for viral reassortment and the emergence of pandemic strains. However, current seasonal influenza vaccines derived from circulating human influenza viruses do not provide protection against human infection with animal influenza A viruses.
